decisions. The broad discretion that the census statute gives to the Secretary 
of Commerce about what questions to include on census forms, and the 
uncertainties of how much of an undercount might be stimulated by including 
the citizenship question, were important factors in the judgment by five 
members of the court that the Secretary had behaved reasonably in making a 
pohcy decision that was his under the statute. In the Chief Justice’s rendering, 
they were also influenced by the long history of asking a citizenship question 
on one or another census form and the potential weaknesses of alternative 
methods for determining how many residents are in fact citizens.
The Justices dissenting on this question, in an opinion authored by Justice 
Breyer, emphasized instead the primary constitutional requirement of the 
census, an accurate enumeration of persons resident within the United States 
and the consensus among experts both within and outside the Department of 
Commerce that the citizenship question would indeed produce an undercount. 
Moreover, the fact that only a modest undercount in certain localities would 
produce loss of a representative in Congress and/or loss of sign-ificAnf. federal 
funds led the dissenters to beheve that it was unreasonable for the Secretary 
to run the imdercount risk that the citizenship question presented. Similar 
disagreements about reasonableness can be observed in case after case in the 
federal courts.
What Department of Commerce v. New York portends for future judicial 
inquiry into the reahty of reasons given by administrators is difficult to gauge. 
Members of the Supreme Court who dissented from the Chief Justice’s 
determination on that question believed that the opinion was opening up a 
legal can of worms (or perhaps a can containing even more dangerous animus) 
that would invite constant attempts to inquire into a  d m i n i str a  tora

motivations beyond what is revealed in administrative records and the 
contemporaneous reasons that administrators provide. To be sure, the Chief 
Justice’s opinion was careful to point out that administrative rationales did not 
have to include all the reasons for an administrative decision or candidly reveal 
all of an administrator’s motives in pursuing a particular policy. The only thing 
required was that the rationale itself be reasonable and that it match the 
record before the reviewing court. The fact that the census case is the first time 
since Overton Park that the Supreme Court has found extra-record pursuit of 
the administrator’s rationale to be justified argues for a limited effect on the 
posture of federal courts in subsequent judicial review proceedings. That those 
disappointed by administrators’ pohcy judgments often suspect ulterior 
motives not revealed by the record makes the dissenters’ fears understandable.
Later cases have refined the standards articulated in Overton Park 
and State Farm. As the next case illustrates, much contemporary judicial 
review focuses on the adequacy and support in the record of the reasons 
provided by an agency for its contested actions.
